summary: Describes situations in S/MIME version 3 where protection against small-subgroup attacks on Diffie-Hellman key agreement is needed, and the methods that can prevent them. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: A cheater can trick a secret handshake into having few choices. This explains how to avoid that trick.

subtitle: When and how S/MIME implementations should defend Diffie-Hellman keys against attackers who send deliberately weak public keys.

tldr.problem: In Diffie-Hellman key agreement, a malicious party can send a public key of small order and, by watching how the victim uses the resulting shared secret, learn part of the victim's private key.
tldr.mechanism: The memo says who needs protection (sender and recipient, depending on whether keys are static or ephemeral) and lists five defenses, such as validating public keys, having the CA validate them, choosing the prime p carefully, and two forms of cofactor exponentiation.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that helps implementers decide whether protection is worth its cost, or whether the application can be engineered so that none is needed.

facts.label: Messages to recover a key
facts.value: As few as about one hundred

facts.label: Public key check
facts.value: y in [2, p-1] and y^q mod p = 1

today: RFC 2785 is an Informational memo published in March 2000 and has not been obsoleted or updated, according to its metadata. It builds on RFC 2631 and the S/MIME version 3 documents.

sections.title: Why Small-Subgroup Attacks Matter
sections.content:
This memo covers the situations in S/MIME version 3 where Diffie-Hellman key agreement (RFC 2631) needs protection from small-subgroup attacks. It focuses on the ephemeral-static and static-static modes. Protection is needed when an attacker could learn a substantial part (more than a few bits) of a user's private key.

Protection has costs: extra processing when a public key is certified or a shared secret is derived, longer parameter generation, and possibly licensing of encumbered technologies. The memo says these must be weighed against engineering the application so that protection is not necessary. It does not worry about a peer who only forces the shared secret to be weak without trying to get the private key, because that peer already knows the secret and could simply publish the plaintext.
sections.eli5: Locking every door costs time and money, so you first ask which doors a burglar could really use. This memo helps you decide.

sections.title: How the Attack Works
sections.content:
The notation follows RFC 2631. The shared secret is ZZ = g ^ (xb * xa) mod p, and each side computes it as (yb ^ xa) mod p or (ya ^ xb) mod p. A static public key is certified and used for more than one key agreement; an ephemeral key is not certified and is used once.

A valid public key has order q. If the other party instead sends a key of small order r, then ZZ can take only r values rather than q-3 values. If Party A encrypts something with ZZ and Party B can see it, or B can tell whether a decryption succeeded, B can search through the r possibilities and learn the private key xa modulo r. The memo says it is not unreasonable to expect the whole private key could be found after as few as one hundred messages.

Two variants are described. A key of the form yb = g^xb * f with f of small order leaks in the same way. A key whose order r factors into small integers lets the attacker use the Pohlig-Hellman algorithm, but this needs the attacker to know ZZ itself, so it is less practical.
sections.eli5: If the cheater's handshake only has a handful of possible answers, the cheater can try them all and see which one matches what you did. Each match gives away a little of your secret.

sections.title: Who Needs Protection
sections.content:
Each party decides independently whether it needs protection. The recipient's key pair is assumed to be static, as it always is in RFC 2631.

Sender. If the sender's key is ephemeral (ephemeral-static Diffie-Hellman), no protection is needed: only recipients could mount the attack, they can already decrypt the message, and no other messages are at risk. If the sender's key is static (static-static), protection is needed, because a recipient could obtain the plaintext sent to another recipient and learn about the sender's private key, which protects other messages too.

Recipient. If absolutely no information about whether decryption worked can reach any other party, no protection is needed, though out of band leaks such as a phone call may still warrant it. If any protocol event lets another party conclude that decryption succeeded, such as replies or returned signed receipts, protection is necessary.
sections.eli5: If you only ever use a throwaway handshake, the cheater learns nothing worth stealing. If you reuse the same handshake, or tell people whether it worked, you should check it carefully.

sections.title: The Five Methods of Protection
sections.content:
The memo lists five measures, and warns that some may be covered by patents or pending patents.

  • Public key validation (from RFC 2631): before computing ZZ, check that the other party's key y lies in the interval [2, p-1] and that y^q mod p equals 1.
  • CA validation: the certification authority performs the same check before issuing a certificate. This works only for static keys, so with ephemeral-static agreement only the sender is protected. Users learn that the CA does this through its Certificate Policy and Certification Practice Statement (RFC 2527) or certificate extensions.
  • Choice of prime p: pick p so that p-1 = 2*q*k with k a large prime or a product of large primes. An element of order 2 remains, so one bit of the private key can still be lost. Choosing p so that k is small leaks only a few bits.
  • Compatible cofactor exponentiation: compute ZZ = (yb^j)^c mod p where c = j^(-1)*xa mod q. It requires gcd(j,q)=1 and gives the same result as ordinary Diffie-Hellman when both keys are valid. If ZZ equals 1, abandon the exchange.
  • Non-compatible cofactor exponentiation: compute ZZ = (yb^j)^xa mod p. The result differs from RFC 2631, so it does not interoperate with conforming implementations. If ZZ equals 1, abandon the exchange.

For both cofactor methods, when j is larger than q (the usual case) they are less efficient than public key validation.
sections.eli5: You can inspect the other person's handshake before using it, ask a trusted office to inspect it for you, build your numbers so there are no weak handshakes, or do some extra math that cancels the weak ones out.

sections.title: Ephemeral-Ephemeral Agreement
sections.content:
When both sides use ephemeral keys, which is not possible in S/MIME but may occur in other protocols, the attacker has more room to work, since both public keys can be changed. For example, the attacker could replace both keys with an element of small order such as -1, so that both sides compute a shared value from a small, easily searched set. Protection may then be needed for both parties.

If the prime was chosen as in the prime-choice method, each user must also make sure the other key is not one of the small-order elements, either by checking a list of them or by adding public key validation or one of the cofactor methods. Protection is unnecessary if the other party's ephemeral public key is authenticated, by a signature, MAC or other integrity protection, as in the Station-To-Station protocol.
sections.eli5: If both people use throwaway handshakes, a sneaky middleman can swap both for weak ones. A signed handshake stops the swap.
